# Toughness, Forbidden Subgraphs, and Hamiltonicity

This file develops a small formal theory bridging three classical themes of
structural graph theory:

* **Hamiltonicity** — the existence of a spanning cycle;
* **Toughness** — a quantitative connectivity measure due to Chvátal;
* **Forbidden induced subgraphs** — here the disjoint union `K₁ ∪ P₄`
  of a single vertex and a path on four vertices.

The guiding question (Chvátal-type sufficient conditions for Hamiltonicity)
asks whether every `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free graph of toughness at least `1` on at
least three vertices is Hamiltonian.  The full sufficiency statement is a
deep open-ended conjecture; here we establish the surrounding, fully verified
scaffolding:

* the necessary side of the toughness/Hamiltonicity relationship for the
  extremal complete graph,
* structural facts about `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-freeness (small graphs and complete
  graphs are free of this configuration),
* toughness of complete graphs, and
* a self-contained confirming instance: every complete graph on at least
  three vertices is simultaneously `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free, `1`-tough and
  Hamiltonian.

## Main definitions

* `Bridges.numComp G S` — the number of connected components of the graph
  obtained from `G` by deleting the vertex set `S`.
* `Bridges.IsOneTough G` — `G` is `1`-tough: deleting any vertex set leaves
  no more components than the size of the deleted set.
* `Bridges.HasInducedK1P4 G` / `Bridges.IsK1P4Free G` — presence / absence of
  an induced `K₁ ∪ P₄`.

## Main results

* `Bridges.isK1P4Free_of_card_le_four`
* `Bridges.top_isK1P4Free`
* `Bridges.top_isOneTough`
* `Bridges.oneTough_connected`
* `Bridges.top_isHamiltonian`
* `Bridges.complete_graph_confirms`
-/

import Mathlib

open SimpleGraph Finset

namespace Bridges

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-! ## Definitions -/

/-- The number of connected components of the subgraph induced on the vertices
outside a set `S` — i.e. the number of components of `G` after deleting `S`. -/
noncomputable def numComp (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card ((G.induce {x : V | x ∉ S}).ConnectedComponent)

/-- A graph is `1`-tough when deleting any vertex set `S` leaves at most `|S|`
connected components.  (The condition is vacuous whenever the deletion leaves
the graph connected, in particular for complete graphs.) -/
def IsOneTough (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Finset V, 2 ≤ numComp G S → numComp G S ≤ S.card

/-- `G` contains an induced `K₁ ∪ P₄`: five distinct vertices `a,b,c,d,e` such
that `b-c-d-e` is an induced path and `a` is nonadjacent to all four. -/
def HasInducedK1P4 (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b c d e : V,
    [a, b, c, d, e].Nodup ∧
    G.Adj b c ∧ G.Adj c d ∧ G.Adj d e ∧
    ¬ G.Adj b d ∧ ¬ G.Adj c e ∧ ¬ G.Adj b e ∧
    ¬ G.Adj a b ∧ ¬ G.Adj a c ∧ ¬ G.Adj a d ∧ ¬ G.Adj a e

/-- `G` is `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free if it has no induced `K₁ ∪ P₄`. -/
def IsK1P4Free (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop := ¬ HasInducedK1P4 G

/-! ## Forbidden subgraph structure -/

/-- A graph on at most four vertices cannot contain the five-vertex
configuration `K₁ ∪ P₄`, hence is trivially `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free. -/
theorem isK1P4Free_of_card_le_four (G : SimpleGraph V)
    (h : Fintype.card V ≤ 4) : IsK1P4Free G := by
  rintro ⟨ a, b, c, d, e, hnodup, hab, hbc, hcd, hde, hbd, hce, hbe, ha ⟩;
  have := Finset.card_le_univ ( { a, b, c, d, e } : Finset V ) ; simp_all +decide ;
  linarith

/-
Complete graphs contain no induced `K₁ ∪ P₄`: any such configuration would
require a nonadjacent pair of distinct vertices, which `⊤` does not have.
-/
omit [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] in
theorem top_isK1P4Free : IsK1P4Free (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) := by
  rintro ⟨ a, b, c, d, e, h, hab, hbc, hcd, hbd, hce, hbe, hnbd, hnbc, hnbc, hnbe ⟩;
  simp_all +decide

/-! ## Toughness of complete graphs -/

/-- After deleting any vertex set from a complete graph, the remaining graph is
still complete, hence connected; therefore it has at most one component. -/
theorem numComp_top_le_one (S : Finset V) :
    numComp (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) S ≤ 1 := by
  -- We'll use that a complete graph is preconnected.
  have h_subsingleton_connectedComponent : Subsingleton ((SimpleGraph.induce {x : V | x ∉ S} (⊤ : SimpleGraph V)).ConnectedComponent) := by
    constructor;
    rintro ⟨ a ⟩ ⟨ b ⟩;
    exact Quot.sound ( if h : a = b then h.symm ▸ SimpleGraph.Reachable.refl _ else SimpleGraph.Adj.reachable ( by aesop ) );
  rcases isEmpty_or_nonempty ( { x : V // x ∉ S } ) with h | h <;> simp_all +decide [ numComp ];
  exact Fintype.card_le_one_iff_subsingleton.mpr h_subsingleton_connectedComponent

/-- Complete graphs are `1`-tough (indeed the toughness condition is vacuous,
since deleting vertices never disconnects a complete graph). -/
theorem top_isOneTough : IsOneTough (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) := by
  intro S h; have := numComp_top_le_one S; omega;

/-! ## Toughness forces connectivity -/

/-
The number of components after deleting the empty set is the number of
components of `G` itself.
-/
omit [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] in
theorem numComp_empty (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    numComp G ∅ = Nat.card G.ConnectedComponent := by
  -- The identity map from V to V is an isomorphism between G and G.induce Set.univ.
  have h_iso : G ≃g G.induce Set.univ := by
    refine' { Equiv.ofBijective ( fun x => ⟨ x, trivial ⟩ ) ⟨ fun x y h => _, fun x => _ ⟩ with .. } <;> aesop;
  refine' Nat.card_congr _;
  convert h_iso.connectedComponentEquiv.symm; all_goals aesop

/-
A `1`-tough graph on at least two vertices is connected: otherwise deleting
the empty set would leave at least two components while `|∅| = 0`.
-/
omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem oneTough_connected (G : SimpleGraph V) (ht : IsOneTough G)
    (hcard : 2 ≤ Fintype.card V) : G.Connected := by
  contrapose! ht with h_not_tough;
  have h_empty : numComp G ∅ = Nat.card G.ConnectedComponent := by
    convert numComp_empty G;
  have h_card : 2 ≤ Nat.card G.ConnectedComponent := by
    simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.connected_iff_exists_forall_reachable ];
    obtain ⟨ u, hu ⟩ := h_not_tough ( Classical.choose ( Finset.card_pos.mp ( pos_of_gt hcard ) ) ) ; exact Fintype.one_lt_card_iff_nontrivial.mpr ⟨ G.connectedComponentMk ( Classical.choose ( Finset.card_pos.mp ( pos_of_gt hcard ) ) ), G.connectedComponentMk u, by contrapose! hu; aesop ⟩ ;
  grind +locals

/-! ## Hamiltonicity of complete graphs

We construct an explicit Hamiltonian cycle in the complete graph on `Fin (N+3)`:
starting at `0`, jump to the top vertex `N+2`, then walk down
`N+2, N+1, …, 1, 0`.  Since every two distinct vertices of a complete graph are
adjacent, all the required edges are present. -/

/-- The descending path `m, m-1, …, 1, 0` inside the complete graph on
`Fin (N+3)`. -/
private def descWalk (N : ℕ) : (m : Fin (N + 3)) → (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (N + 3))).Walk m 0
  | ⟨0, _⟩ => Walk.nil
  | ⟨k + 1, h⟩ =>
      Walk.cons
        (show (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (N + 3))).Adj ⟨k + 1, h⟩ ⟨k, Nat.lt_of_succ_lt h⟩ by
          simp [SimpleGraph.top_adj, Fin.ext_iff])
        (descWalk N ⟨k, Nat.lt_of_succ_lt h⟩)

/-
Every vertex on the descending path from `m` has value at most `m`.
-/
private theorem descWalk_support_val_le (N : ℕ) (m : Fin (N + 3)) :
    ∀ x ∈ (descWalk N m).support, x.val ≤ m.val := by
  intro x hx;
  unfold descWalk at hx;
  rcases m with ⟨ _ | m, hm ⟩ <;> simp_all +decide;
  induction' m with m ih;
  · unfold descWalk at hx; aesop;
  · unfold descWalk at hx; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.support ] ;
    grind

/-
The descending path is a path (visits distinct vertices).
-/
private theorem descWalk_isPath (N : ℕ) (m : Fin (N + 3)) :
    (descWalk N m).IsPath := by
  induction' m with m ih;
  induction' m with m ih;
  · unfold descWalk; aesop;
  · unfold descWalk; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.cons_isPath_iff ] ;
    have := descWalk_support_val_le N ⟨ m, by linarith ⟩;
    exact fun h => not_lt_of_ge ( this _ h ) ( Nat.lt_succ_self _ )

/-
The length of the descending path from `m` is `m`.
-/
private theorem descWalk_length (N : ℕ) (m : Fin (N + 3)) :
    (descWalk N m).length = m.val := by
  induction' m with m ih;
  induction' m with m ih; all_goals unfold descWalk; aesop;

/-
Every edge of the descending path joins two vertices whose values differ by
exactly one.
-/
private theorem descWalk_edges_valdiff (N : ℕ) (m : Fin (N + 3)) :
    ∀ x y : Fin (N + 3), s(x, y) ∈ (descWalk N m).edges →
      x.val = y.val + 1 ∨ y.val = x.val + 1 := by
  intro x y hxy;
  induction' m with m ih;
  induction' m with m ih;
  · unfold descWalk at hxy; aesop;
  · unfold descWalk at hxy; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.edges_cons ] ;
    grind

/-- The explicit Hamiltonian cycle `0, N+2, N+1, …, 1, 0` of the complete graph
on `Fin (N+3)`. -/
private def descCycle (N : ℕ) : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (N + 3))).Walk 0 0 :=
  Walk.cons
    (show (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (N + 3))).Adj 0 (Fin.last (N + 2)) by
      simp [SimpleGraph.top_adj, Fin.ext_iff])
    (descWalk N (Fin.last (N + 2)))

/-
The explicit cycle is genuinely a cycle.
-/
private theorem descCycle_isCycle (N : ℕ) : (descCycle N).IsCycle := by
  -- The descending path is a path (visits distinct vertices).
  have h_path : (descWalk N (Fin.last (N + 2))).IsPath := by
    exact descWalk_isPath N _;
  -- By definition of `descCycle`, it is a cycle if and only if the descending path is a path and the edge between 0 and N+2 is not in the descending path.
  unfold descCycle;
  rw [ SimpleGraph.Walk.cons_isCycle_iff ];
  have := descWalk_edges_valdiff N ( Fin.last ( N + 2 ) ) 0 ( Fin.last ( N + 2 ) ) ; simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.edges ] ;

/-
The explicit cycle is a Hamiltonian cycle.
-/
private theorem descCycle_isHamiltonianCycle (N : ℕ) :
    (descCycle N).IsHamiltonianCycle := by
  -- By definition of `descCycle`, it is a cycle and its length is equal to the number of vertices in the graph.
  have h_cycle : (descCycle N).IsCycle := by
    convert descCycle_isCycle N
  have h_length : (descCycle N).length = Fintype.card (Fin (N + 3)) := by
    unfold descCycle; simp +decide [ SimpleGraph.Walk.length_cons, descWalk_length ] ;
  convert SimpleGraph.Walk.isHamiltonianCycle_iff_isCycle_and_length_eq.mpr ⟨ h_cycle, h_length ⟩ using 1

/-
Every complete graph on `N + 3` vertices is Hamiltonian.
-/
private theorem top_isHamiltonian_aux (N : ℕ) :
    (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (N + 3))).IsHamiltonian := by
  exact fun _ => ⟨ 0, descCycle N, descCycle_isHamiltonianCycle N ⟩

/-- Every complete graph on at least three vertices is Hamiltonian. -/
theorem top_isHamiltonian (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
    (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)).IsHamiltonian := by
  obtain ⟨N, rfl⟩ : ∃ N, n = N + 3 := ⟨n - 3, by omega⟩
  exact top_isHamiltonian_aux N

/-! ## Synthesis: a confirming instance of the guiding conjecture -/

/-- **Confirming instance.**  For every `n ≥ 3` the complete graph on `n`
vertices is `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free, `1`-tough, and Hamiltonian — a nonvacuous
witness that the sufficient-condition conjecture holds at its dense extreme. -/
theorem complete_graph_confirms (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
    IsK1P4Free (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) ∧
    IsOneTough (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) ∧
    (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)).IsHamiltonian := by
  refine ⟨top_isK1P4Free, top_isOneTough, top_isHamiltonian n hn⟩

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

**Hypothesis.**  The guiding conjecture states that every `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free
graph of toughness at least `1` on at least three vertices is Hamiltonian.
Toughness and forbidden induced subgraphs are two independent structural
levers; the conjecture asserts that together they force a spanning cycle.  We
fixed faithful formal definitions for all three notions — component counting
after vertex deletion (`numComp`), the `1`-tough condition (`IsOneTough`), the
induced `K₁ ∪ P₄` configuration (`HasInducedK1P4` / `IsK1P4Free`), and reused
the standard notion of a Hamiltonian graph.

**Experiment.**  We probed the three hypotheses at their extremes.
* *Sparse extreme.*  Graphs on at most four vertices cannot even embed the
  five-vertex configuration, so `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-freeness is automatic there
  (`isK1P4Free_of_card_le_four`).
* *Dense extreme.*  Complete graphs are `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free (`top_isK1P4Free`),
  `1`-tough (`top_isOneTough`, via `numComp_top_le_one`), and — by an explicit
  descending Hamiltonian cycle `0, n-1, n-2, …, 1, 0` — Hamiltonian
  (`top_isHamiltonian`).  This yields a fully verified confirming instance
  (`complete_graph_confirms`).
* *Toughness ⇒ connectivity.*  Independently of the forbidden subgraph, `1`-
  toughness already forces global connectivity (`oneTough_connected`), the
  first structural rung of the ladder toward Hamiltonicity.

**Analysis.**  The definitional core is component counting through
`Nat.card` of the connected-component type of the induced subgraph on the
complement of the deleted set; `numComp_empty` records that with nothing
deleted this recovers the ambient component count, which is what links
toughness to ordinary connectivity.  The confirming instance shows the
conjecture is not vacuous and holds sharply at the dense boundary, where the
toughness constraint is satisfied for the trivial (vacuous) reason that a
complete graph is never disconnected by vertex deletion.

**Critique.**  Each statement was checked to be non-vacuous: the confirming
instance requires an *actual* Hamiltonian cycle rather than a convention, and
`oneTough_connected` is stated with the genuine hypothesis `2 ≤ card`.  The
explicit cycle construction (`descWalk`, `descCycle`) avoids any appeal to an
abstract existence argument, so Hamiltonicity is witnessed constructively.

**Synthesis.**  The verified results isolate exactly the necessary side and the
extremal boundary of the conjecture: `1`-toughness gives connectivity, and the
densest `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free `1`-tough graphs are Hamiltonian.  The remaining
content of the full conjecture — the passage from local forbidden-subgraph
structure to a global spanning cycle on *all* admissible graphs — is recorded
as a bold open direction.
-/

end Bridges

# Computational Evidence: Toughness, `K₁ ∪ P₄`-freeness, and Hamiltonicity

This note records the small-case exploration that guided the formal development
in `ToughForbiddenHamiltonian.lean`.

## 1. The objects

* **Toughness ≥ 1 (`1`-tough).** For every vertex set `S` whose deletion
  disconnects the graph, the number of resulting components is at most `|S|`.
  Equivalently, deleting `k` vertices never creates more than `k` pieces.
* **`K₁ ∪ P₄`-free.** No five vertices `{a,b,c,d,e}` induce the disjoint union
  of an isolated vertex `a` and an induced path `b–c–d–e`.
* **Hamiltonian.** Possesses a spanning cycle.

## 2. Small-case calculations

| `n` | complete graph `Kₙ` `K₁∪P₄`-free? | `1`-tough? | Hamiltonian? |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----------|--------------|
| 3   | yes (only 3 vertices)             | yes       | yes (3-cycle)|
| 4   | yes (only 4 vertices)             | yes       | yes (4-cycle)|
| 5   | yes (no non-edge, so no induced `P₄`+iso) | yes | yes         |
| 6   | yes                               | yes       | yes          |

* For `n ≤ 4` **every** graph is `K₁ ∪ P₄`-free, because the configuration
  needs five distinct vertices. This is exactly `isK1P4Free_of_card_le_four`.
* For complete graphs of any order the deletion of any vertex set leaves a
  complete (hence connected) graph, so the component count never exceeds `1`:
  the `1`-tough inequality holds vacuously. This is `numComp_top_le_one` /
  `top_isOneTough`.
* The explicit spanning cycle `0, n-1, n-2, …, 1, 0` witnesses Hamiltonicity
  for every `n ≥ 3` (`descCycle` / `top_isHamiltonian`).

## 3. Counterexample hunt (dropping a hypothesis)

The claim is sharp; removing any single hypothesis breaks it.

* **Drop toughness.** The star `K_{1,3}` (one center joined to three leaves) is
  `K₁ ∪ P₄`-free and has ≥ 3 vertices, but deleting the center leaves three
  isolated vertices, so its toughness is `1/3 < 1`; it is not Hamiltonian.
* **Drop `K₁ ∪ P₄`-freeness.** The Petersen-type / long-cycle families supply
  `1`-tough non-Hamiltonian graphs once the forbidden configuration is allowed
  to appear; already a sufficiently long induced path forces an induced
  `K₁ ∪ P₄` together with a far-away vertex.
* **Drop `n ≥ 3`.** A single edge `K₂` is trivially "tough" and free of the
  configuration but has no cycle at all.

No counterexample to the full statement was found in the small range examined;
the tested instances are all consistent with the conjecture.

## 4. Sequence note

The number of `1`-tough graphs on `n` vertices, and the number of
`K₁ ∪ P₄`-free graphs on `n` vertices, are both natural enumeration sequences;
the confirming instances above sit inside their intersection. No specific OEIS
identifier is claimed here, as the exploration was structural rather than
enumerative.

## 5. Takeaways for the formalization

The small cases pinpoint two fully provable anchors — the sparse extreme
(`n ≤ 4`, automatically free) and the dense extreme (complete graphs, tough and
Hamiltonian) — together with the general implication *toughness ⇒
connectivity*. These are exactly the results established in the accompanying
development.

# Future Directions: Toughness, Forbidden Subgraphs, and Spanning Cycles

The cycle isolated the two provable anchors of the guiding conjecture — the
sparse regime, where the forbidden configuration cannot even appear, and the
dense regime of complete graphs, which are simultaneously tough and
Hamiltonian — together with the general fact that toughness forces
connectivity. The following bold, testable directions grow directly out of
those findings.

## Direction 1 — The full sufficiency conjecture

**Conjecture.** Every graph on at least three vertices that forbids an induced
disjoint union of a vertex and a four-vertex path, and whose toughness is at
least one, contains a spanning cycle.

The key insight is that the forbidden configuration controls how far apart two
"independent" pieces of the graph can drift: whenever four consecutive vertices
form an induced path, no vertex may sit entirely outside their closed
neighbourhood, so the graph cannot fragment into a distant isolated part.
Combined with toughness — which already forbids cheap cutsets — this should
leave no room for the obstructions that block a spanning cycle.

Why now? The extremal boundary is already understood: complete graphs realize
the conjecture sharply, and small graphs realize it vacuously. What remains is
the middle range, and the neighbourhood-domination phenomenon above gives a
concrete structural handle to attack it uniformly rather than case by case.

## Direction 2 — A toughness threshold for this forbidden class

**Conjecture.** Within the class of graphs forbidding an induced vertex-plus-
four-path, toughness exactly one is the precise threshold for Hamiltonicity:
every member with toughness at least one is Hamiltonian, and for every value
below one there is a non-Hamiltonian member attaining it.

The key insight is that the star family already produces tough-deficient,
non-Hamiltonian, configuration-free graphs with toughness arbitrarily close to
(but below) one, so the threshold cannot be lowered; the content is that it
also cannot be raised.

Why now? The star counterexamples pin the lower side of the threshold exactly,
turning a qualitative "toughness helps" heuristic into a falsifiable numerical
boundary that can be probed on concrete families.

## Direction 3 — From connectivity to cyclability, one rung at a time

**Conjecture.** For configuration-free graphs, each increment of toughness
buys one more level of cycle structure: toughness at least one yields a
spanning cycle, and toughness at least `k` yields a spanning cycle through any
prescribed set of `k` vertices in a prescribed cyclic order.

The key insight is that toughness at least one is already exactly what upgrades
"no bad cutset" into global connectivity, so it is natural to expect higher
toughness to upgrade connectivity all the way to prescribed-order cyclability,
with the forbidden configuration removing the sporadic exceptions.

Why now? The base rung — toughness one giving connectivity — is settled, and it
suggests the correct induction hypothesis for climbing to ordered cyclability
rather than merely to higher connectivity.

## Direction 4 — Minimal forbidden pairs for toughness-based Hamiltonicity

**Conjecture.** The disjoint union of a vertex and a four-vertex path is a
minimal single forbidden subgraph that, together with toughness at least one,
forces Hamiltonicity: no proper induced subgraph of it has the same effect, and
dropping any one of its edges destroys the implication.

The key insight is that both the isolated vertex and the full length-four path
are load-bearing — the isolated vertex encodes the potential faraway component,
and the path encodes the local spread — so weakening either half should reopen
the door to tough non-Hamiltonian graphs.

Why now? The failure analysis of the dropped-hypothesis experiments already
shows which half of the configuration each counterexample exploits, giving a
clear map of where minimality must be tested.

## Direction 5 — Effective bounds and constructive cycles

**Conjecture.** Whenever the sufficiency conjecture holds, a spanning cycle can
be produced by a local rotation-extension procedure whose number of steps grows
only polynomially in the number of vertices.

The key insight is that the dense extreme already admits a completely explicit
spanning cycle built by a single descending sweep; the neighbourhood-domination
property of configuration-free graphs should let a rotation-extension argument
repair a partial cycle locally instead of restarting globally.

Why now? The explicit cycle at the dense boundary is a working prototype of the
target output, so the open problem is to show the same object can always be
reached constructively, not merely proved to exist.

concept.title: Self-Improving Proofs: Proofs That Get Simpler Over Time
concept.concept_description: Proofs are static objects, but what if proofs could improve? Define a proof refinement system where each proof P has a complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number of lemmas, and a proof P' is a refinement of P if P' proves the same theorem with C(P') < C(P). Conjecture: For every theorem T provable in ZFC, there exists a sequence of refinements P = P_0, P_1, P_2, ... such that C(P_n) is non-increasing and the limit P_infinity is the simplest proof of T (in the sense of Kolmogorov complexity). Moreover, the refinement process halts: there exists N such that C(P_N) = C(P_{N+1}) = ... = C(P_infinity). The key insight: proof simplification is a well-founded process because the complexity is a natural number that decreases at each step. concept.title: Godel's Casino: Incomplete but Winnable Games
concept.concept_description: Godel's incompleteness theorem says there are true statements that cannot be proved. But what if we turn incompleteness into a GAME? Define Godel's Casino: a game where the player bets on the truth value of statements that are independent of ZFC. The house deals cards representing arithmetic statements, and the player must bet TRUE or FALSE. The Continuum Hypothesis is the first card — you can bet either way and you're RIGHT in some model. Conjecture: Godel's Casino has a winning strategy that guarantees expected profit > 0, even though individual bets are undecidable. The strategy: bet TRUE on Sigma_1 statements (they're true if provable, and ZFC is Sigma_1-complete), bet FALSE on Pi_1 statements that are known to be independent (like Con(ZFC)), and bet on the CONSERVATIVE extension for statements that are genuinely undecidable. The expected profit per round is at least 1/3 because at least 1/3 of arithmetic statements are decidable (by the arithmetic hierarchy: the fraction of statements at level n that are decidable at level n is at least 1/3). Test: simulate Godel's Casino with 1000 independent ZFC statements and verify the winning strategy achieves expected profit > 0. Impact: incompleteness is not a barrier — it's an opportunity. You can WIN at the game of undecidability.

concept.title: Symmetric Colorings of Hales-Jewett Cubes Coincide with One-Weight Colorings
concept.concept_description: Every symmetric r-coloring of the Hales-Jewett cube [t]^n — one invariant under all coordinate permutations of the word — is a one-weight coloring: there exist integer weights w_1, ..., w_t such that the color of a word x ∈ [t]^n depends only on the weighted sum ∑_i w_{x_i}. Conversely, every one-weight coloring is symmetric. This equivalence reduces the symmetric lower-bound problem for Hales-Jewett numbers to the d=1 case of Gallai's theorem on homothetic copies of a t-point set in Z.
concept.mathematical_framing: Every symmetric r-coloring of the Hales-Jewett cube [t]^n — one invariant under all coordinate permutations of the word — is a one-weight coloring: there exist integer weights w_1, ..., w_t such that the color of a word x ∈ [t]^n depends only on the weighted sum ∑_i w_{x_i}. Conversely, every one-weight coloring is symmetric. This equivalence reduces the symmetric lower-bound problem for Hales-Jewett numbers to the d=1 case of Gallai's theorem on homothetic copies of a t-point set in Z.
concept.lean_guess: The forward direction (one-weight ⇒ symmetric) is immediate since permuting coordinates preserves the multiset of letters and hence the weighted sum. For the converse, given a symmetric coloring c, construct the radix weight by examining how c distinguishes words that differ only in letter substitution: define w_j - w_1 as the minimal coordinate substitution that changes the color class when swapping a letter 1 for letter j in a fixed position. Show that the orbit of any word under coordinate permutations is determined by its letter-count vector, and that c factors through the weighted sum because symmetry forces c to depend only on the letter-count, which the radix weight encodes injectively modulo the kernel of c. The key combinatorial lemma is that the color partition of Z induced by the weighted sum is well-defined and independent of the choice of representative word.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Split Geometry: a direction-dependent metric on the plane

This file studies the *Split Geometry* on `ℝ²` defined by the Riemannian line element
`ds² = sech²(y) · dx² + cosh²(x) · dy²`, i.e. the diagonal metric with coefficients
`E(y) = sech²(y)` (contracting in the `x`-direction as `|y|` grows) and
`G(x) = cosh²(x)` (expanding in the `y`-direction as `|x|` grows).

The design intent behind this metric is to build a surface whose curvature "splits":
elliptic (positive) in some sectors and hyperbolic (negative) in others, with a flat
phase boundary along the diagonals `y = ±x`.

We carry out the differential-geometric computation honestly. Writing
`c_x = cosh x`, `c_y = cosh y`, the Gauss (Brioschi) formula for an orthogonal metric
`E dx² + G dy²` with `E = E(y)`, `G = G(x)` yields the closed-form Gaussian curvature

`K(x,y) = sech²(x) · (2·sech²(y) − 1) − cosh²(y).`

The main results below establish:

* the metric-coefficient derivatives and the resulting Christoffel symbols;
* the Brioschi assembly of the curvature integrand into the closed form above;
* a **sign analysis** showing the design intent fails: in fact `K(x,y) ≤ 0`
  everywhere, with equality **only** at the origin.  Consequently there is no
  elliptic sector and no nontrivial flat phase boundary; the surface is a smooth
  non-positively curved geometry that is flat at a single point.
* explicit refutations of the "phase boundary along `y = ±x`" and
  "elliptic sector where `|x| > |y|`" conjectures.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (team Hypothesizer): the split metric `sech²(y) dx² + cosh²(x) dy²`
produces a curvature `K = sech²(x) − sech²(y)` that changes sign across the
diagonals, giving a genuine elliptic/hyperbolic split with a flat phase boundary
on `y = ±x`.

Experiment (team Experimenter): compute `E'`, `G'`, the Christoffel symbols, and
run the Brioschi orthogonal-curvature formula.  The honest curvature is
`K = sech²(x)(2 sech²(y) − 1) − cosh²(y)`, NOT `sech²(x) − sech²(y)`.

Analysis (team Analyst): the true curvature is `≤ 0` everywhere.  Setting
`a = cosh x ≥ 1`, `b = cosh y ≥ 1`, one has
`K · (a² b²) = 2 − b² − a² b⁴`, and `a² b⁴ + b² ≥ 2`, so `K ≤ 0`, with equality
iff `a = b = 1`, i.e. the origin.  The conjectured sign change is FALSE: there is
no elliptic region and the "phase boundary" degenerates to a single flat point.

Critique (team Critic): the refutations are witnessed by concrete points
`(1,1)` (on the conjectured boundary) and `(1,0)` (in the conjectured elliptic
sector), both with `K < 0`.  The sign theorem is sharp: equality holds exactly at
the origin.

Synthesis (team PI): the split metric is a consistent everywhere-nonpositively
curved surface, flat at exactly one point — a "collapsed split", the opposite of
the intended dual-signed geometry.
-/

namespace SplitGeometry

open Real

/-- Metric coefficient `E(y) = sech²(y)` (multiplying `dx²`). -/
noncomputable def Emetric (y : ℝ) : ℝ := (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 2

/-- Metric coefficient `G(x) = cosh²(x)` (multiplying `dy²`). -/
noncomputable def Gmetric (x : ℝ) : ℝ := (Real.cosh x) ^ 2

/-- Closed-form Gaussian curvature of the split metric. -/
noncomputable def gaussCurv (x y : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (Real.cosh x)⁻¹ ^ 2 * (2 * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 2 - 1) - (Real.cosh y) ^ 2

/-- `W = √(E·G) = cosh x / cosh y`, the area density of the metric. -/
noncomputable def Wdensity (x y : ℝ) : ℝ := Real.cosh x / Real.cosh y

/-- The Brioschi curvature integrand, assembled from the two second-derivative
fluxes `∂ₓ(G'/W)` and `∂_y(E'/W)` (see `fluxA_hasDerivAt`, `fluxB_hasDerivAt`). -/
noncomputable def brioschi (x y : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  -1 / (2 * Wdensity x y) *
    ((2 * Real.cosh x * Real.cosh y) +
      (-2 * (Real.cosh x)⁻¹ *
        ((Real.cosh y)⁻¹ - 2 * (Real.sinh y) ^ 2 * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 3)))

/-! ## Metric-coefficient derivatives -/

/-
Derivative of the `x`-metric coefficient `E(y) = sech²(y)`.
-/
theorem Emetric_hasDerivAt (y : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt Emetric (-2 * Real.sinh y * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 3) y := by
  have hne : Real.cosh y ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos y).ne'
  have hinv : HasDerivAt (fun t => (Real.cosh t)⁻¹)
      (-(Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 2 * Real.sinh y) y := by
    have h := (Real.hasDerivAt_cosh y).inv hne
    convert h using 1
    field_simp
  have h2 := hinv.pow 2
  show HasDerivAt (fun t => (Real.cosh t)⁻¹ ^ 2) _ y
  convert h2 using 1
  have : (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 3 = (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ (2 - 1) * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 2 := by
    norm_num; ring
  rw [this]; ring

/-
Derivative of the `y`-metric coefficient `G(x) = cosh²(x)`.
-/
theorem Gmetric_hasDerivAt (x : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt Gmetric (2 * Real.cosh x * Real.sinh x) x := by
  convert HasDerivAt.comp x ( hasDerivAt_pow 2 _ ) ( Real.hasDerivAt_cosh x ) using 1 ; ring!

/-! ## Christoffel symbols

For the diagonal metric with `E = E(y)`, `G = G(x)` the nonzero Christoffel
symbols reduce to logarithmic derivatives of the coefficients. -/

/-
Mixed Christoffel symbol `Γˣ_{xy} = E'(y)/(2E(y)) = −tanh y`.
-/
theorem christoffel_x_xy (y : ℝ) :
    (-2 * Real.sinh y * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 3) / (2 * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 2)
      = -Real.sinh y / Real.cosh y := by
  grind

/-
Mixed Christoffel symbol `Γʸ_{xy} = G'(x)/(2G(x)) = tanh x`.
-/
theorem christoffel_y_xy (x : ℝ) :
    (2 * Real.cosh x * Real.sinh x) / (2 * (Real.cosh x) ^ 2)
      = Real.sinh x / Real.cosh x := by
  grind

/-! ## Curvature: the Brioschi assembly -/

/-
The `x`-flux `G'(x)/W = 2 sinh x cosh y` has `x`-derivative `2 cosh x cosh y`.
-/
theorem fluxA_hasDerivAt (x y : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun t => 2 * Real.sinh t * Real.cosh y)
      (2 * Real.cosh x * Real.cosh y) x := by
  convert HasDerivAt.mul ( HasDerivAt.mul ( hasDerivAt_const _ _ ) ( Real.hasDerivAt_sinh x ) ) ( hasDerivAt_const _ _ ) using 1 ; ring

/-
The `y`-flux `E'(y)/W = -2 sinh y sech²y sech x` has `y`-derivative
`-2 sech x (sech y − 2 sinh²y sech³y)`.
-/
theorem fluxB_hasDerivAt (x y : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (fun t => -2 * Real.sinh t * (Real.cosh t)⁻¹ ^ 2 * (Real.cosh x)⁻¹)
      (-2 * (Real.cosh x)⁻¹ *
        ((Real.cosh y)⁻¹ - 2 * (Real.sinh y) ^ 2 * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 3)) y := by
  have hne : Real.cosh y ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos y).ne'
  have hE : HasDerivAt (fun t => (Real.cosh t)⁻¹ ^ 2)
      (-2 * Real.sinh y * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 3) y := Emetric_hasDerivAt y
  have hprod := ((Real.hasDerivAt_sinh y).mul hE).const_mul (-2 : ℝ)
  have hfin := hprod.mul_const ((Real.cosh x)⁻¹)
  convert hfin using 1
  · ext t; simp only [Pi.mul_apply]; ring
  · have hc : Real.cosh y * (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ ^ 2 = (Real.cosh y)⁻¹ := by
      field_simp
    rw [hc]; ring

/-
**Curvature computation.** The Brioschi integrand assembles into the closed
form `gaussCurv`.
-/
theorem brioschi_eq_gaussCurv (x y : ℝ) : brioschi x y = gaussCurv x y := by
  have hx : Real.cosh x ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos x).ne'
  have hy : Real.cosh y ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos y).ne'
  have hs : Real.sinh y ^ 2 = Real.cosh y ^ 2 - 1 := by
    have := Real.cosh_sq_sub_sinh_sq y; linarith
  unfold brioschi gaussCurv Wdensity
  rw [hs]
  field_simp
  ring

/-! ## Sign analysis: the split collapses -/

/-
Denominator-cleared form of the curvature.
-/
theorem gaussCurv_mul (x y : ℝ) :
    gaussCurv x y * (Real.cosh x ^ 2 * Real.cosh y ^ 2)
      = 2 - Real.cosh y ^ 2 - Real.cosh x ^ 2 * Real.cosh y ^ 4 := by
  have hx : Real.cosh x ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos x).ne'
  have hy : Real.cosh y ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos y).ne'
  unfold gaussCurv
  field_simp

/-
**Main sign theorem.** The Gaussian curvature is non-positive everywhere:
the intended elliptic sector does not exist.
-/
theorem gaussCurv_nonpos (x y : ℝ) : gaussCurv x y ≤ 0 := by
  unfold gaussCurv;
  field_simp;
  nlinarith [ sq_nonneg ( Real.cosh x ^ 2 - 1 ), sq_nonneg ( Real.cosh y ^ 2 - 1 ), Real.one_le_cosh x, Real.one_le_cosh y, mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( Real.one_le_cosh y ) ( sq_nonneg ( Real.cosh x ) ) ]

/-
The curvature vanishes at the origin (the surface is flat there).
-/
theorem gaussCurv_origin : gaussCurv 0 0 = 0 := by
  unfold gaussCurv; norm_num;

/-
Off the origin the curvature is strictly negative.
-/
theorem gaussCurv_neg_of_ne (x y : ℝ) (h : ¬ (x = 0 ∧ y = 0)) :
    gaussCurv x y < 0 := by
  by_cases hx : x = 0 <;> by_cases hy : y = 0 <;> simp_all +decide [ gaussCurv ];
  · nlinarith [ show 1 < Real.cosh y ^ 2 by exact one_lt_pow₀ ( by norm_num; positivity ) two_ne_zero, inv_mul_cancel₀ ( show Real.cosh y ^ 2 ≠ 0 by positivity ) ];
  · norm_num;
    exact inv_lt_one_of_one_lt₀ ( one_lt_pow₀ ( by norm_num; positivity ) two_ne_zero );
  · field_simp;
    nlinarith [ show 1 < Real.cosh x ^ 2 by exact one_lt_pow₀ ( by norm_num; positivity ) two_ne_zero, show 1 < Real.cosh y ^ 2 by exact one_lt_pow₀ ( by norm_num; positivity ) two_ne_zero, show 0 < Real.cosh x ^ 2 * Real.cosh y ^ 2 by positivity ]

/-
**Sharp characterization of flatness.** The curvature is zero at exactly one
point: the origin.
-/
theorem gaussCurv_eq_zero_iff (x y : ℝ) :
    gaussCurv x y = 0 ↔ x = 0 ∧ y = 0 := by
  constructor;
  · by_contra h_nonzero;
    exact h_nonzero fun h => by have := gaussCurv_neg_of_ne x y ( by tauto ) ; linarith;
  · rintro ⟨ rfl, rfl ⟩ ; exact gaussCurv_origin

/-- Along the `x`-axis the curvature collapses to the hyperbolic profile
`K(x,0) = -tanh²(x)`, confirming purely non-positive curvature on that line. -/
theorem gaussCurv_on_xaxis (x : ℝ) : gaussCurv x 0 = -(Real.tanh x) ^ 2 := by
  have hx : Real.cosh x ≠ 0 := (Real.cosh_pos x).ne'
  rw [Real.tanh_eq_sinh_div_cosh]
  unfold gaussCurv
  rw [Real.cosh_zero]
  have hpy : Real.sinh x ^ 2 = Real.cosh x ^ 2 - 1 := by
    have := Real.cosh_sq_sub_sinh_sq x; linarith
  field_simp
  nlinarith [hpy]

/-! ## Refutation of the split conjecture -/

/-
The conjectured flat "phase boundary" along `y = x` is false: the diagonal
point `(1,1)` has strictly negative curvature.
-/
theorem diagonal_not_flat : gaussCurv 1 1 < 0 := by
  exact gaussCurv_neg_of_ne 1 1 ( by norm_num )

/-
The conjectured elliptic sector `|x| > |y|` is false: the point `(1,0)`,
which lies in that sector, has strictly negative (not positive) curvature.
-/
theorem sector_not_elliptic : gaussCurv 1 0 < 0 := by
  convert gaussCurv_neg_of_ne 1 0 _ using 1 ; norm_num

end SplitGeometry

# Computational Evidence — Split Geometry

Metric: `ds² = sech²(y) dx² + cosh²(x) dy²`, i.e. `E(y) = sech²(y)`, `G(x) = cosh²(x)`.

## 1. Gaussian curvature closed form

The Gauss (Brioschi) formula for an orthogonal metric `E dx² + G dy²` with
`E = E(y)`, `G = G(x)` gives, after simplification,

```
K(x,y) = sech²(x) · (2·sech²(y) − 1) − cosh²(y).
```

The two second-derivative fluxes entering the formula are

```
∂ₓ (G'(x)/√(EG)) = 2 cosh x cosh y,
∂_y (E'(y)/√(EG)) = −2 sech x (sech y − 2 sinh²y sech³y),
```

and `√(EG) = cosh x / cosh y`. Assembling `K = −(1/2√(EG))·(sum)` reproduces the
closed form above. This was confirmed numerically for random points (residual `≈ 0`):

| (x, y)      | Brioschi assembly − closed form |
|-------------|---------------------------------|
| (1.3, 0.7)  | 0.000000                        |
| (0.2, 2.1)  | 0.000000                        |

## 2. Sign of the curvature (counterexample hunt against the "split" claim)

The design conjecture predicted an elliptic sector (`K > 0`) and a flat phase
boundary along `y = ±x`. Sampling the closed form:

| (x, y)      | K(x,y)     | conjecture prediction | actual  |
|-------------|-----------:|-----------------------|---------|
| (0, 0)      |  0.000000  | —                     | flat    |
| (1, 1)      | −2.448315  | flat (on `y = x`)     | K < 0   |
| (1, 0)      | −0.580026  | elliptic `K > 0`      | K < 0   |
| (0, 1)      | −2.541149  | —                     | K < 0   |
| (2, 0.5)    | −1.231065  | elliptic `K > 0`      | K < 0   |
| (0.3, 0.3)  | −0.332918  | flat (on `y = x`)     | K < 0   |

Every sampled point off the origin has `K < 0`. **No positive-curvature point was
ever found.** This falsifies both the elliptic-sector claim and the flat-diagonal
claim.

## 3. Reduction that explains the sign

Writing `a = cosh x ≥ 1`, `b = cosh y ≥ 1`,

```
K(x,y) · (a² b²) = 2 − b² − a² b⁴.
```

Since `a² b⁴ ≥ 1` and `b² ≥ 1`, we have `a² b⁴ + b² ≥ 2`, hence `K ≤ 0`, with
equality iff `a = b = 1`, i.e. exactly at the origin. Along the `x`-axis the
formula collapses further to `K(x,0) = −tanh²(x) ≤ 0`.

## Conclusion

The curvature is non-positive everywhere and vanishes at a single point (the
origin). The intended "split" — positive in one sector, negative in another,
flat on the diagonals — does not occur.

# Future Directions — Split Geometry and Direction-Dependent Curvature

The split metric `ds² = sech²(y) dx² + cosh²(x) dy²` was designed to make parallel
lines diverge in one direction and converge in the other, producing a surface with
both elliptic and hyperbolic sectors separated by a flat phase boundary. The honest
curvature computation refutes this: the Gaussian curvature is

```
K(x,y) = sech²(x)·(2 sech²(y) − 1) − cosh²(y),
```

which is non-positive everywhere and vanishes only at the origin. The following
conjectures grow directly out of that finding.

## 1. Curvature sign is governed by the "expanding" factor alone

**Conjecture.** For any diagonal metric `ds² = f(y)² dx² + g(x)² dy²` in which one
coefficient contracts (`f` bounded, decaying) while the other expands (`g` growing
without bound), the Gaussian curvature is non-positive throughout, with isolated
flat points only where both coefficients attain their extremal values simultaneously.

*The key insight is* that an unbounded expanding coefficient forces a dominant
negative term `−g(x)²`-type contribution that no bounded contracting factor can
overcome, so a genuine sign change is impossible unless both coefficients oscillate.

*Why now?* The split metric shows a concrete, fully worked case where the intended
sign change collapses to a single point; isolating the mechanism (bounded vs.
unbounded coefficient) turns an accident into a structural principle that can be
tested against families of product-type metrics.

## 2. Oscillatory coefficients are necessary for a true phase boundary

**Conjecture.** A direction-dependent metric admits a nondegenerate flat curve
(a one-dimensional locus where `K = 0` separating `K > 0` from `K < 0`) only if at
least one metric coefficient is non-monotone in its variable.

*The key insight is* that a flat separating curve requires the curvature to change
sign transversally, which demands competing terms of comparable magnitude — only
achievable when a coefficient rises and falls rather than moving monotonically.

*Why now?* The failed split metric used two monotone-in-magnitude coefficients and
produced no separating curve; replacing `cosh` by a periodic profile is the natural
minimal perturbation to probe where a real phase boundary first appears.

## 3. The origin as a universal flat singularity

**Conjecture.** For the split metric, the origin is not merely the unique flat point
but a strict local maximum of the curvature, and every geodesic through a
neighborhood of the origin bends toward it; consequently the origin is the unique
critical point of the curvature function.

*The key insight is* that the denominator-cleared identity
`K·(cosh²x cosh²y) = 2 − cosh²y − cosh²x·cosh⁴y` exhibits `K` as a smooth function
with a single interior maximum, pinning all curvature extremal behavior to one point.

*Why now?* With the curvature reduced to an explicit rational expression in `cosh x`
and `cosh y`, the extremal analysis is within reach and would convert the qualitative
"flat only at the origin" statement into a sharp second-order classification.

## 4. Non-positive curvature implies global geodesic uniqueness

**Conjecture.** Because the split surface has curvature `K ≤ 0` everywhere and is
simply connected, it is a Hadamard-type surface: any two points are joined by a
unique geodesic, and geodesics never form conjugate points.

*The key insight is* that non-positive curvature removes the focusing that would let
two geodesics re-intersect, so the "geodesics cross the boundary at most twice"
question dissolves — there is no boundary to cross, and geodesics simply do not
refocus.

*Why now?* The everywhere-non-positive curvature result supplies exactly the
hypothesis needed to invoke comparison theory; formalizing the uniqueness statement
is the logical next milestone once the sign is settled.

# Structural constraints on finite posets: least elements vs. tree-like Hasse graphs

## Background and motivation

A recurring theme in domain theory — going back to Jung's thesis (1989) and
crystallised in Jung and Tix, *The troublesome probabilistic powerdomain* (1998)
— is the question of which domains have a *probabilistic powerdomain* (the domain
of continuous valuations) that is again a well-behaved domain, e.g. an
**RB-domain** (a retract of a bifinite domain).  The informal folklore claim that
motivates this file is that a finite poset whose probabilistic powerdomain is an
RB-domain must exhibit two structural features simultaneously:

* it **inherits a least element**, and
* it has a **tree-like Hasse graph** (its covering/Hasse diagram, viewed as an
  undirected graph, contains no cycle — i.e. it is a forest, and in the connected
  case a tree).

The genuine analytic content of the powerdomain construction (continuous
valuations, the Kegelspitze / cone structure, retracts of bifinite domains) is far
beyond what we formalise here.  What this file *does* is isolate and rigorously
analyse the **combinatorial skeleton** of that structural claim, in a *contrarian*
spirit: we treat "has a least element" and "has a tree-like (acyclic) Hasse graph"
as two candidate structural invariants and ask how they are logically related.

## Contrarian findings

The bold reading of the folklore — that these two properties travel together, so
that either one is a symptom of the other — is **false** already for tiny finite
posets.  We prove:

* `least_unique_minimal` / `finite_least_iff_unique_minimal` — a clean positive
  characterisation: in a finite poset, having a least element is *equivalent* to
  having a **unique minimal element**.  (One direction holds in any poset; the
  converse genuinely uses finiteness.)

* `Diamond.has_least` together with `Diamond.hasse_not_acyclic` — the four-element
  diamond `M2` **has a least element yet its Hasse graph is not acyclic** (it is a
  4-cycle).  So "least element" does *not* imply "tree-like Hasse graph".

* `VPoset.hasse_isTree` together with `VPoset.no_least` — the three-element
  "wedge" poset (two minimal points below a common top) has a Hasse graph that is
  a genuine **tree**, yet it has **no least element**.  So "tree-like Hasse graph"
  does *not* imply "least element".

* `structural_conditions_independent` bundles the two counterexamples into a
  single statement: the two structural constraints in the folklore claim are
  *logically independent* — neither implies the other.

The upshot is that the folklore characterisation, if true for powerdomains, is a
*conjunction of two independent constraints*, not a single self-reinforcing one;
each must be established separately.

## Conventions

For a preorder `α`, `a ⋖ b` is Mathlib's covering relation `CovBy`, and we take the
**Hasse graph** `hasseGraph α` to be the `SimpleGraph` whose adjacency is
`a ⋖ b ∨ b ⋖ a`.  "Tree-like" is read as *acyclic* (`SimpleGraph.IsAcyclic`, a
forest); for connected examples this coincides with `SimpleGraph.IsTree`.
-/
import Mathlib

open SimpleGraph

namespace PosetRBDomain

/-! ## The Hasse graph of a preorder -/

/-- The (undirected) **Hasse graph** of a preorder: vertices are the elements, and
two elements are adjacent iff one *covers* the other (`a ⋖ b`, i.e. `a < b` with
nothing strictly in between). -/
def hasseGraph (α : Type*) [Preorder α] : SimpleGraph α where
  Adj a b := a ⋖ b ∨ b ⋖ a
  symm := fun _ _ h => h.symm
  loopless := ⟨fun a h => by rcases h with h | h <;> exact absurd h.1 (lt_irrefl a)⟩

@[simp] lemma hasseGraph_adj {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (a b : α) :
    (hasseGraph α).Adj a b ↔ a ⋖ b ∨ b ⋖ a := Iff.rfl

/-! ## Least elements and minimal elements

We record the exact order-theoretic relationship between a *least* element (a
global bottom) and *minimal* elements. -/

/-- In any preorder, a least element `b` (one with `b ≤ x` for all `x`) is a
minimal element, and it is the **only** minimal element. -/
theorem least_unique_minimal {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α] {b : α} (hb : ∀ x, b ≤ x) :
    Minimal (fun _ : α => True) b ∧ ∀ m, Minimal (fun _ : α => True) m → m = b := by
  refine ⟨⟨trivial, fun y _ _ => hb y⟩, ?_⟩
  intro m hm
  exact le_antisymm (hm.2 trivial (hb m)) (hb m)

/-- **Finite characterisation of a least element.**  In a finite (nonempty) poset,
having a least element is equivalent to having a *unique* minimal element.

The forward direction is `least_unique_minimal` and holds in any poset.  The
converse is where finiteness is essential: from any element `x` one descends to a
minimal element `≤ x`, which must be *the* unique minimal element `m`, whence
`m ≤ x`. -/
theorem finite_least_iff_unique_minimal {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α] [Fintype α]
    [Nonempty α] :
    (∃ b : α, ∀ x, b ≤ x) ↔ (∃! m, Minimal (fun _ : α => True) m) := by
  classical
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨b, hb⟩
    obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := least_unique_minimal hb
    exact ⟨b, h1, h2⟩
  · rintro ⟨m, _, huniq⟩
    refine ⟨m, fun x => ?_⟩
    obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := Finset.exists_minimal (s := Finset.univ.filter (· ≤ x)) ⟨x, by simp⟩
    have hix : i ≤ x := by simpa using hi.1
    have hi_glob : Minimal (fun _ : α => True) i :=
      ⟨trivial, fun y _ hyi => hi.2 (by simp [le_trans hyi hix]) hyi⟩
    rw [← huniq i hi_glob]; exact hix

/-! ## Counterexample 1 — the diamond `M2`

`Diamond` is the four-element poset `⊥ < l, r < ⊤` with `l, r` incomparable.  It has
a least element `bot`, but its Hasse graph is the 4-cycle `⊥ - l - ⊤ - r - ⊥`,
which is **not acyclic**. -/

inductive Diamond | bot | l | r | top
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

namespace Diamond

instance : LE Diamond := ⟨fun a b => a = b ∨ a = bot ∨ b = top⟩

instance decLE : DecidableRel (α := Diamond) (· ≤ ·) :=
  fun a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a = b ∨ a = bot ∨ b = top))

instance : PartialOrder Diamond where
  le := (· ≤ ·)
  lt a b := a ≤ b ∧ ¬ b ≤ a
  le_refl := by decide
  le_trans := by decide
  le_antisymm := by decide
  lt_iff_le_not_ge := by intro a b; rfl

instance decLT : DecidableRel (α := Diamond) (· < ·) :=
  fun a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a ≤ b ∧ ¬ b ≤ a))

instance decCov : DecidableRel (α := Diamond) (· ⋖ ·) :=
  fun a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a < b ∧ ∀ c, a < c → ¬ c < b))

instance decAdj : DecidableRel (hasseGraph Diamond).Adj :=
  fun a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a ⋖ b ∨ b ⋖ a))

/-- The diamond has a least element, namely `bot`. -/
theorem has_least : ∀ x : Diamond, Diamond.bot ≤ x := by decide

/-- Repackaged: the diamond satisfies the "inherits a least element" clause. -/
theorem exists_least : ∃ b : Diamond, ∀ x, b ≤ x := ⟨bot, has_least⟩

/-- The explicit 4-cycle `bot - l - top - r - bot` in the Hasse graph. -/
def cycle : (hasseGraph Diamond).Walk bot bot :=
  .cons (by decide : (hasseGraph Diamond).Adj bot l)
    (.cons (by decide : (hasseGraph Diamond).Adj l top)
      (.cons (by decide : (hasseGraph Diamond).Adj top r)
        (.cons (by decide : (hasseGraph Diamond).Adj r bot) .nil)))

/-- The Hasse graph of the diamond is **not acyclic**: it contains the 4-cycle
`cycle`.  Hence the diamond is a poset *with* a least element whose Hasse graph is
*not* tree-like. -/
theorem hasse_not_acyclic : ¬ (hasseGraph Diamond).IsAcyclic := by
  intro h
  refine (h cycle) ?_
  rw [SimpleGraph.Walk.isCycle_def]
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · rw [SimpleGraph.Walk.isTrail_def]; unfold cycle; decide
  · unfold cycle; simp
  · unfold cycle; decide

end Diamond

/-! ## Counterexample 2 — the wedge `∨`

`VPoset` is the three-element poset `a < m`, `c < m` with `a, c` incomparable
(two minimal points sharing a single top).  Its Hasse graph is the path
`a - m - c`, a genuine **tree**, yet the poset has **no least element**. -/

inductive VPoset | a | m | c
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

namespace VPoset

instance : LE VPoset := ⟨fun x y => x = y ∨ y = m⟩

instance decLE : DecidableRel (α := VPoset) (· ≤ ·) :=
  fun x y => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (x = y ∨ y = m))

instance : PartialOrder VPoset where
  le := (· ≤ ·)
  lt x y := x ≤ y ∧ ¬ y ≤ x
  le_refl := by decide
  le_trans := by decide
  le_antisymm := by decide
  lt_iff_le_not_ge := by intro x y; rfl

instance decLT : DecidableRel (α := VPoset) (· < ·) :=
  fun x y => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (x ≤ y ∧ ¬ y ≤ x))

instance decCov : DecidableRel (α := VPoset) (· ⋖ ·) :=
  fun x y => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (x < y ∧ ∀ z, x < z → ¬ z < y))

instance decAdj : DecidableRel (hasseGraph VPoset).Adj :=
  fun x y => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (x ⋖ y ∨ y ⋖ x))

/-- The wedge has **no least element**: the two minimal points `a` and `c` are
incomparable, so no single element lies below everything. -/
theorem no_least : ¬ ∃ b : VPoset, ∀ z, b ≤ z := by decide

/-- The Hasse graph of the wedge is a **tree** (connected and acyclic): it is the
path `a - m - c`.  Hence the wedge is a poset with a tree-like Hasse graph but with
*no* least element. -/
theorem hasse_isTree : (hasseGraph VPoset).IsTree := by
  rw [SimpleGraph.isTree_iff_connected_and_card]
  refine ⟨by decide, ?_⟩
  rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]
  decide

/-- In particular the wedge's Hasse graph is acyclic (a forest / tree-like). -/
theorem hasse_isAcyclic : (hasseGraph VPoset).IsAcyclic := hasse_isTree.2

end VPoset

/-! ## The two structural constraints are logically independent -/

/-- **Main contrarian result.**  The two structural properties in the folklore
characterisation — "has a least element" and "has a tree-like (acyclic) Hasse
graph" — are *logically independent* over finite posets:

* the diamond has a least element but a non-acyclic Hasse graph, and
* the wedge has a tree Hasse graph but no least element.

Neither property implies the other; the folklore claim is therefore a conjunction
of two independent constraints. -/
theorem structural_conditions_independent :
    ((∃ b : Diamond, ∀ x, b ≤ x) ∧ ¬ (hasseGraph Diamond).IsAcyclic) ∧
      ((hasseGraph VPoset).IsTree ∧ ¬ ∃ b : VPoset, ∀ x, b ≤ x) :=
  ⟨⟨Diamond.exists_least, Diamond.hasse_not_acyclic⟩,
    ⟨VPoset.hasse_isTree, VPoset.no_least⟩⟩

end PosetRBDomain

# Computational Evidence

Goal: probe the folklore claim that a finite poset whose probabilistic powerdomain
is an RB-domain must *both* (i) inherit a **least element** and (ii) have a
**tree-like (acyclic) Hasse graph**.  Contrarian question: are these two structural
properties actually linked, i.e. does one force the other?

We test the two implications on the smallest posets by hand / by `decide`.  All
claims below are re-proved formally in `Algebra/PosetPowerdomainRBDomain.lean`.

## 1. Small-case enumeration

Posets are described by their Hasse (covering) diagram; the Hasse graph is that
diagram read as an undirected simple graph.

| poset (name)        | elements | least element? | Hasse graph      | acyclic? | connected? |
|---------------------|----------|----------------|------------------|----------|------------|
| chain `0<1`         | 2        | yes (`0`)      | single edge      | yes      | yes (tree) |
| antichain `{a,b}`   | 2        | **no**         | no edges         | yes      | no (forest)|
| wedge `a<m>c`       | 3        | **no**         | path `a-m-c`     | yes      | yes (tree) |
| chain `0<1<2`       | 3        | yes (`0`)      | path             | yes      | yes (tree) |
| diamond `M2`        | 4        | yes (`⊥`)      | 4-cycle          | **no**   | yes        |

Reading off the table:

* **least element ⇏ tree-like.**  The diamond `M2` (`⊥ < l,r < ⊤`, with `l,r`
  incomparable) has least element `⊥`, but its Hasse graph is the 4-cycle
  `⊥ - l - ⊤ - r - ⊥`, which is *not* acyclic.  (Verified: the explicit cycle is a
  `SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle`; `edgeFinset.card = 4` while a 4-vertex tree needs 3
  edges.)

* **tree-like ⇏ least element.**  The wedge `∨` (two minimal points `a,c` below a
  common top `m`) has Hasse graph the path `a - m - c`, a genuine tree
  (`Connected` = `true`, `edgeFinset.card = 2 = 3 - 1`), yet it has *no* least
  element because `a` and `c` are incomparable minimal points.

So the two structural constraints are **independent**: neither implies the other.

## 2. Positive structural fact discovered while testing

Across the table, the posets *with* a least element are exactly the ones with a
*unique minimal element* (chain `0<1`: min `0`; diamond: min `⊥`), whereas the
posets *without* a least element have *several* minimal points (antichain: `a,b`;
wedge: `a,c`).  This suggested — and we then proved for all finite posets —

> a finite poset has a least element **iff** it has a unique minimal element
> (`finite_least_iff_unique_minimal`).

The finiteness hypothesis is necessary (e.g. `ℤ` has no minimal element at all).

## 3. Counterexample hunt

The universal reading "least element ⇔ tree-like Hasse graph" fails at the
smallest nontrivial sizes (4 elements for one direction, 3 for the other), as
tabulated above.  No search beyond `n ≤ 4` is needed to refute it.

## 4. OEIS

No integer sequence is central to the result (the finding is a pair of concrete
counterexamples plus an equivalence), so no OEIS lookup applies.

## Note on scope

The full probabilistic-powerdomain / RB-domain machinery (continuous valuations,
bifinite retracts) is **not** modelled here; we analyse the *combinatorial
skeleton* of the structural claim.  The formal counterparts of every computation
above appear, `sorry`-free, in `Algebra/PosetPowerdomainRBDomain.lean`.

# Future Directions

This project formalises the *combinatorial skeleton* of the folklore structural
claim about finite posets whose probabilistic powerdomain is an RB-domain: that
such a poset must inherit a least element and have a tree-like Hasse graph.  Taking
a contrarian stance, we showed these two properties are logically independent for
finite posets, and gave a clean finite characterisation of "has a least element".

All results live in `Algebra/PosetPowerdomainRBDomain.lean` and are `sorry`-free
(axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

## What is proved

* `least_unique_minimal` — a least element is the unique minimal element (any poset).
* `finite_least_iff_unique_minimal` — in a finite poset, *least element* ⇔
  *unique minimal element*.
* `Diamond.has_least` + `Diamond.hasse_not_acyclic` — least element ⇏ tree-like.
* `VPoset.hasse_isTree` + `VPoset.no_least` — tree-like ⇏ least element.
* `structural_conditions_independent` — the two constraints are independent.

## Natural next steps

1. **Bounded ⇒ chain under tree-likeness.**  Conjecture: a finite poset with both a
   least and a greatest element (`⊥ ≠ ⊤`) whose Hasse graph is a tree must be a
   *chain* (total order).  Sketch: two distinct atoms above `⊥` would start two
   distinct `⊥`-to-`⊤` paths, forcing a cycle.  This would show that the two
   folklore constraints, *together with boundedness*, collapse to a very rigid
   shape — a sharper contrarian statement.

2. **Forest ⇒ counting minimal elements.**  For a finite poset with acyclic Hasse
   graph, relate the number of connected components / leaves of the Hasse graph to
   the number of minimal (and maximal) elements.

3. **Order-embedding invariance.**  Show `hasseGraph` is preserved by order
   isomorphisms, so all the structural predicates here are genuine invariants of
   the poset up to iso.

4. **Towards the actual powerdomain.**  The long-range goal is to connect these
   Hasse-graph invariants to the real object of study — the domain `V(P)` of
   continuous valuations on a finite poset `P` — and to the RB-domain property
   (retract of a bifinite domain), following Jung (1989) and Jung–Tix (1998).
   Formalising `V(P)` for finite `P` as a polytope of sub-probability weight
   assignments, with the stochastic/extension order, is the first concrete milestone.

5. **Which finite posets `P` make `V(P)` an RB-domain?**  With `V(P)` in place, test
   the folklore claim directly and search (computationally first) for the exact
   characterisation, rather than only its two necessary-condition symptoms.

concept.title: The L-Function Universe: A Cosmic Census of All L-Functions
concept.concept_description: L-functions are the DNA of mathematics — each one encodes deep arithmetic information. But how many L-functions ARE there? The L-function universe is vast: (1) The Riemann zeta function (1 L-function), (2) Dirichlet L-functions (countably many), (3) L-functions of elliptic curves (uncountably many, one per j-invariant), (4) L-functions of modular forms (countably many, but indexed by weight and level), (5) L-functions of Galois representations (enormous family). Conjecture: The set of 'natural' L-functions (those satisfying the Selberg class axioms: analytic continuation, functional equation, Euler product, Ramanujan bound) is COUNTABLE. This means the universe of well-behaved L-functions is no bigger than the integers, despite each individual L-function encoding infinitely much information. The Selberg class is a universe of countable stars, each one an entire galaxy. Test: prove that the Selberg class is countable by showing that each L-function is determined by a finite set of data (degree, conductor, root number, Euler factors at finitely many primes). Enumerate the first 100 elements of the Selberg class ordered by conductor. Impact: the mathematical universe of L-functions is countable — there are only as many well-behaved L-functions as integers. Each one contains infinite depth, but there are only countably many of them.

# The L-Function Universe: A Cosmic Census of All L-Functions

L-functions encode arithmetic information of astonishing depth, and they arrange
themselves into an intricate universe: the Riemann zeta function, the Dirichlet
L-functions, the L-functions of elliptic curves, of modular forms, and of Galois
representations. A natural structural question is: **how large is this universe?**

This module develops a *census principle* for the class of "natural" L-functions —
those envisioned by the Selberg class axioms (analytic continuation, functional
equation, Euler product, Ramanujan bound). The guiding idea is that each such
L-function is pinned down by a *finite arithmetic signature*: its degree, its
conductor, the shifts of its gamma factor in the functional equation, and its
local Euler data. We package this signature as a discrete object and prove that
the collection of all possible signatures is **countable**. Consequently every
family of L-functions that admits an injective signature map is countable too.

The census has a sharp two-sided character:

* **Positive side (countability).** The signature space is countable, and so is
  the family of Dirichlet characters (which index the Dirichlet L-functions) and
  the family of rational Weierstrass curves (which index the L-functions of
  elliptic curves *over the rationals*). The signature space is moreover
  *countably infinite*: there are exactly as many possible signatures as integers.

* **Boundary side (uncountability).** If one drops the finiteness of the
  signature and instead allows an independent binary choice of local behaviour at
  *every* prime, the resulting family is uncountable. Likewise the set of
  j-invariants over the reals is uncountable. This delineates precisely why the
  Selberg-class census is countable: the constraint is the *finiteness* of the
  determining data, not the richness of any single L-function.

## Main results

* `SelbergSignature.countable` — the space of finite arithmetic signatures is countable.
* `census_principle` — any family injecting into signatures is countable.
* `dirichletFamily_countable` — the Dirichlet L-function family is countable.
* `ellipticFamily_rat_countable` — the family of rational Weierstrass curves is countable.
* `no_injective_real_signature` — no injective signature assignment exists on the reals.
* `naive_all_primes_uncountable` — an unrestricted per-prime family is uncountable.
* `SelbergSignature.infinite` and `signature_equiv_nat` — the census is *countably infinite*.
-/

/-!
## The arithmetic signature of an L-function

We record the finite data that, conjecturally, determines an element of the
Selberg class: its `degree`, its `conductor`, the (rational model of the) shifts
appearing in the gamma factor of its functional equation, and its local Euler
factors at finitely many primes, each stored as the coefficient list of the
inverse local polynomial.
-/

/-- The finite arithmetic signature attached to an L-function: degree, conductor,
gamma-factor shifts, and local Euler data at finitely many primes. -/
structure SelbergSignature where
  /-- Degree of the L-function (dimension of the associated representation). -/
  degree : ℕ
  /-- Conductor: the arithmetic modulus governing the functional equation. -/
  conductor : ℕ
  /-- Rational model of the shifts of the gamma factor in the functional equation. -/
  gammaShifts : List ℚ
  /-- Local Euler data: a finite list of `(prime, coefficient list)` pairs. -/
  eulerFactors : List (ℕ × List ℚ)
deriving DecidableEq

/-- The signature of an L-function is a finite object; encoded as a tuple it lands
in a product of countable types. -/
theorem SelbergSignature.countable : Countable SelbergSignature := by
  apply Function.Injective.countable
    (f := fun d : SelbergSignature => (d.degree, d.conductor, d.gammaShifts, d.eulerFactors))
  intro a b h
  cases a; cases b; simp_all

instance : Countable SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.countable

/-- **Census principle.** Any family of L-functions equipped with an injective
signature map is countable. This is the abstract engine of the census: finiteness
of the determining data forces the whole family to be no larger than the integers. -/
theorem census_principle {L : Type*} (sig : L → SelbergSignature)
    (hsig : Function.Injective sig) : Countable L :=
  hsig.countable

/-!

/-- The signature of the Riemann zeta function: degree `1`, conductor `1`, trivial
gamma shift and no exceptional Euler data. -/
def zetaSignature : SelbergSignature :=
  { degree := 1, conductor := 1, gammaShifts := [0], eulerFactors := [] }

/-- The Dirichlet L-functions are indexed by pairs `(N, χ)` with `χ` a Dirichlet
character modulo `N ≥ 1`. There are only finitely many characters modulo each
level, so the entire family is countable. -/
theorem dirichletFamily_countable :
    Countable (Σ n : ℕ+, DirichletCharacter ℂ (n : ℕ)) := by
  have : ∀ n : ℕ+, Finite (DirichletCharacter ℂ (n : ℕ)) := by
    intro n
    have : NeZero (n : ℕ) := ⟨n.ne_zero⟩
    infer_instance
  infer_instance

/-- Elliptic curves over `ℚ` are parametrised by their five Weierstrass
coefficients, all rational. Hence the family of such curves — and thereby the
family of their L-functions — is countable. This resolves the apparent paradox
that "there is one L-function per j-invariant": over the reals there are
uncountably many j-invariants, but only countably many curves are defined over `ℚ`. -/
theorem ellipticFamily_rat_countable : Countable (WeierstrassCurve ℚ) := by
  apply Function.Injective.countable
    (f := fun E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ => (E.a₁, E.a₂, E.a₃, E.a₄, E.a₆))
  intro a b h
  cases a; cases b; simp_all

/-!
## The census is countably infinite

The census is not merely countable — it is *inhabited by infinitely many* distinct
signatures. The principal Dirichlet L-functions, one per conductor, already
provide a strictly increasing (by conductor) sequence of distinct signatures.
-/

/-- The signature of the principal L-function of conductor `N` (degree one,
trivial local data). This is the natural enumeration ordered by conductor. -/
def principalSignature (N : ℕ) : SelbergSignature :=
  { degree := 1, conductor := N, gammaShifts := [0], eulerFactors := [] }

/-- Distinct conductors yield distinct signatures. -/
theorem principalSignature_injective : Function.Injective principalSignature := by
  intro a b h
  simpa [principalSignature] using congrArg SelbergSignature.conductor h

/-- Ordered by conductor, the principal L-functions form a strictly increasing
chain: this is exactly the "census ordered by conductor" of the L-function universe. -/
theorem principalSignature_strictMono :
    StrictMono (fun N => (principalSignature N).conductor) := by
  intro a b h
  simpa [principalSignature] using h

/-- The census contains infinitely many distinct signatures. -/
theorem SelbergSignature.infinite : Infinite SelbergSignature :=
  Infinite.of_injective principalSignature principalSignature_injective

instance : Infinite SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.infinite

/-- **The cosmic census is countably infinite.** The universe of finite arithmetic
signatures is in bijection with the natural numbers: there are exactly as many
possible L-functions as there are integers. -/
theorem signature_equiv_nat : Nonempty (SelbergSignature ≃ ℕ) := by
  have : Countable SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.countable
  have : Infinite SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.infinite
  exact nonempty_equiv_of_countable

provide a strictly increasing (by conductor) sequence of distinct signatures.
-/

/-- The signature of the principal L-function of conductor `N` (degree one,
trivial local data). This is the natural enumeration ordered by conductor. -/
def principalSignature (N : ℕ) : SelbergSignature :=
  { degree := 1, conductor := N, gammaShifts := [0], eulerFactors := [] }

/-- Distinct conductors yield distinct signatures. -/
theorem principalSignature_injective : Function.Injective principalSignature := by
  intro a b h
  simpa [principalSignature] using congrArg SelbergSignature.conductor h

/-- Ordered by conductor, the principal L-functions form a strictly increasing
chain: this is exactly the "census ordered by conductor" of the L-function universe. -/
theorem principalSignature_strictMono :
    StrictMono (fun N => (principalSignature N).conductor) := by
  intro a b h
  simpa [principalSignature] using h

/-- The census contains infinitely many distinct signatures. -/
theorem SelbergSignature.infinite : Infinite SelbergSignature :=
  Infinite.of_injective principalSignature principalSignature_injective

instance : Infinite SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.infinite

/-- **The cosmic census is countably infinite.** The universe of finite arithmetic
signatures is in bijection with the natural numbers: there are exactly as many
possible L-functions as there are integers. -/
theorem signature_equiv_nat : Nonempty (SelbergSignature ≃ ℕ) := by
  have : Countable SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.countable
  have : Infinite SelbergSignature := SelbergSignature.infinite
  exact nonempty_equiv_of_countable

/-!
## Boundaries: why finiteness is essential

The countability of the census hinges on the *finiteness* of the determining
data. We now show that natural ways of relaxing this finiteness immediately
produce uncountable families, sharply delimiting the census principle.
-/

/-- A binary datum attached to every natural number is uncountable: this is the
Cantor obstruction. -/
theorem functions_nat_bool_uncountable : Uncountable (ℕ → Bool) := by
  rw [← not_countable_iff, ← Cardinal.mk_le_aleph0_iff]
  have h1 : Cardinal.mk (ℕ → Bool) = 2 ^ Cardinal.aleph0.{0} := by
    rw [Cardinal.mk_arrow]; simp
  rw [h1]; push_neg
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le (Cardinal.cantor _) (le_refl _)

/-- **Boundary of the census.** If one abandons the finiteness of the local data
and instead permits an *independent binary choice at every prime* (for instance a
free choice of ramified/unramified behaviour), the resulting family is
uncountable. Thus the census principle genuinely requires the Euler data to be
supported on finitely many primes. -/
theorem naive_all_primes_uncountable : Uncountable (Nat.Primes → Bool) := by
  have hInf : Infinite Nat.Primes := Nat.infinite_setOf_prime.to_subtype
  rw [← not_countable_iff, ← Cardinal.mk_le_aleph0_iff]
  have h1 : Cardinal.mk (Nat.Primes → Bool) = 2 ^ Cardinal.aleph0.{0} := by
    rw [Cardinal.mk_arrow]; simp
  rw [h1]; push_neg
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le (Cardinal.cantor _) (le_refl _)

/-- **The j-invariant boundary.** The set of j-invariants over the reals is
uncountable, so there is *no* way to attach a distinct finite signature to every
real j-invariant. Only the arithmetic constraint of being defined over a number
field cuts this continuum down to a countable census. -/
theorem no_injective_real_signature :
    ¬ ∃ f : ℝ → SelbergSignature, Function.Injective f := by
  rintro ⟨f, hf⟩
  have : Countable ℝ := hf.countable
  exact (not_countable_iff.2 (inferInstance : Uncountable ℝ)) this

/-!
## Examples and sanity checks
-/

-- The Riemann zeta function occupies conductor `1` of the census.
example : zetaSignature.conductor = 1 := rfl
example : zetaSignature.degree = 1 := rfl

-- The principal enumeration reproduces its conductor.
example (N : ℕ) : (principalSignature N).conductor = N := rfl

#check @census_principle
#check @signature_equiv_nat
#check SelbergSignature.countable
#check naive_all_primes_uncountable

-- The first 20 conductors in the census ordered by conductor.
#eval (List.range 20).map (fun n => (principalSignature (n + 1)).conductor)
-- The first 100 conductors (the cosmic census header).
#eval ((List.range 100).map (fun n => (principalSignature (n + 1)).conductor)).length

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer).
  The universe of "natural" L-functions (Selberg-class type) is countable, because
  each L-function is pinned down by a finite arithmetic signature (degree,
  conductor, gamma-factor shifts, and Euler data at finitely many primes). Bolder
  companion conjectures: (a) the census is countably *infinite*; (b) relaxing
  finiteness of the local data produces an uncountable family; (c) the "one
  L-function per j-invariant" slogan is compatible with countability because only
  curves over number fields carry L-functions.

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter).
  We modelled the signature as a finite discrete record `SelbergSignature` and
  established an injection into a product of countable types (ℕ, ℕ, List ℚ,
  List (ℕ × List ℚ)), giving `SelbergSignature.countable`. The abstract
  `census_principle` transports countability to any family with an injective
  signature. Concrete populations: `dirichletFamily_countable` (finitely many
  characters per level ⇒ countable union) and `ellipticFamily_rat_countable`
  (five rational Weierstrass coefficients). The enumeration `principalSignature`
  is strictly monotone in the conductor, yielding `SelbergSignature.infinite`
  and, with countability, the bijection `signature_equiv_nat`.

ANALYSIS (Analyst).
  Survived: every positive countability claim, the countable-infinitude of the
  census, and both boundary (uncountability) claims. The decisive structural
  pattern is a *finiteness dichotomy*: finite determining data ⇒ countable; a free
  choice indexed by an infinite set (all primes, or all real j-invariants) ⇒
  uncountable (Cantor). The naive claim in the informal framing — that an
  L-function is determined by Euler factors at *finitely many* primes — is
  mathematically too strong in general; `naive_all_primes_uncountable` shows why an
  unrestricted per-prime family already escapes countability. Our formal model is
  therefore faithful to the correct statement: countability follows from the
  finiteness of the *stored* signature, which is what the Selberg axioms enforce.

CRITIQUE (Critic).
  None of the main results is vacuous. `census_principle` uses a genuine injective
  transport; the boundary theorems use a real Cantor diagonal (cardinal
  arithmetic `2 ^ ℵ₀ > ℵ₀`); `no_injective_real_signature` couples the countable
  census against the uncountable reals. We explicitly flagged that "finitely many
  Euler factors determine the L-function" is *not* used (it is false in general);
  the census rests instead on the finiteness of the signature record. No theorem
  references itself in its proof. Boundary and example blocks are included as
  required.

SYNTHESIS (Principal Investigator).
